An equality condition for the Dobrushin bound on attention rollout and how often it holds in trained transformers

Przemysław Rola ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Kraków University of Economics, e-mail: przemyslaw.rola@outlook.com
Abstract

The Dobrushin coefficient of each attention-rollout factor satisfies κ⁡(12​(I+A))≤12​(1+κ⁡(A))\kappa(\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A))\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\kappa(A)), and multiplying these inequalities over layers bounds the coefficient of the whole rollout. We characterise exactly when the layerwise bound is tight: equality holds if and only if some token pair attaining κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) is mutually self-dominant — each of the two attends to itself at least as strongly as the other attends to it. The condition is far from automatic: uniformly random stochastic matrices satisfy it only 2424–30%30\% of the time.

When tested on the head-averaged attention of each individual input and restricted to content tokens — image patches, words or tabular features, excluding cls, register and separator tokens — the condition holds for essentially every input at every layer of DINOv2 (three model sizes), RoBERTa and DistilBERT. In the supervised models DeiT-B and ViT-B/16 it holds for 91%91\% and 64%64\% of input–layer pairs respectively, with all failures occurring late in depth. In FT-Transformer trained on two standard tabular benchmarks it holds for only 1111–44%44\% of input–layer pairs. The special tokens account for almost all failures in DINOv2 and the language models: when they are included, the condition holds for only 8282–97%97\% of input–layer pairs.

††footnotetext: 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 68T07, 60J10, 15B51. Key words and phrases. Attention rollout, Dobrushin coefficient, stochastic matrices, residual connections, transformers, attention sinks.

1 Introduction

In a transformer, each attention layer mixes tokens. For every token it forms a weighted average of all tokens’ value vectors — the weights being one row of a row-stochastic attention matrix — and adds the result to that token’s representation. Information is thereby redistributed across positions and the representations are pulled toward one another. Iterating this aggregation can drive all tokens toward a common representation — rank collapse in the vision and language literature (Dong et al., 2021), oversmoothing in the graph setting (Oono and Suzuki, 2020; Wu et al., 2023). Whether, and how fast, a given trained network approaches that regime is a question about a product of many mixing operators, one per layer.

Attention rollout (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020) is the standard way to summarise such a product. It multiplies the attention matrices of successive layers into a single row-stochastic operator describing how attention-mediated influence accumulates with depth. To account for the residual (skip) connection, which passes each token’s representation to the next layer unchanged, each attention matrix AA is first replaced by 12​(I+A)\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A), the identity II standing for the skip connection. Because the result is row-stochastic, the classical theory of products of inhomogeneous stochastic matrices applies to it directly.

Biccari et al. (2026) make that connection explicit. They analyse rollout with Doeblin–Dobrushin contraction theory, show that an operator with a small Dobrushin coefficient is quantitatively close to a rank-one matrix, and control the coefficient of the composed operator by a layerwise estimate: writing A~=12​(I+A)\widetilde{A}=\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A) for a rollout factor, κ⁡(A~)≤12​(1+κ⁡(A))\kappa(\widetilde{A})\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1+\kappa(A)\big), which composes across LL layers into a certificate carrying a factor 2−L2^{-L}. They also prove an unconditional lower bound κ⁡(A~)≥(N−2)/(2​(N−1))\kappa(\widetilde{A})\geq(N-2)/(2(N-1)) on any single factor, and observe empirically that the composed coefficient decreases with depth in trained tabular transformers.

Their treatment therefore brackets the coefficient of each factor, κ⁡(A~(ℓ))\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}), from above and from below, but leaves a question unanswered: when is the upper bound an equality? The question is not cosmetic. If the estimate is loose, the depth certificate built from it may be improvable layer by layer, and the numbers it produces say more about the estimate than about the network. If it is tight, no layer’s estimate can be improved; the depth certificate may still overstate the coefficient of the whole rollout, but only because the coefficient of a product of matrices can be smaller than the product of their coefficients.

This paper answers when the layerwise bound is an equality, and draws out the consequences. Throughout, the object is the row-stochastic attention matrix AA — the token-mixing pattern — rather than the full multi-head attention block of a layer, X↦∑hAh​X​WhV​WhOX\mapsto\sum_{h}A_{h}XW_{h}^{V}W_{h}^{O} (Vaswani et al., 2017), which also includes the value and output projections,11 1 In the notation of Vaswani et al. (2017), the multi-head block of a self-attention layer, which all models here use, is Concat⁡(head1,…,headH)​WO\mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_{1},\dots,\mathrm{head}_{H})\,W^{O} with headh=Attention⁡(X​WhQ,X​WhK,X​WhV)=Ah​X​WhV\mathrm{head}_{h}=\mathrm{Attention}(XW_{h}^{Q},XW_{h}^{K},XW_{h}^{V})=A_{h}XW_{h}^{V}, where XX is the input of the block and AhA_{h} is head hh’s row-stochastic attention matrix. Splitting WOW^{O} into the row blocks WhOW_{h}^{O} belonging to the heads turns the product into the sum ∑hheadh​WhO\sum_{h}\mathrm{head}_{h}\,W_{h}^{O}. Biases add the same vector to every token, since each AhA_{h} has rows summing to one, and so do not affect the token-mixing pattern. so none of what follows certifies the complete computation; (M1) in Section 2 states this formally.

Contributions.

(i) An exact characterisation of when the layerwise bound of Biccari et al. (2026) is an equality (Proposition 2). (ii) A test of the condition on the object their bound uses, the head-averaged attention matrix of each input: on content tokens it holds for essentially every input at every layer of DINOv2 and of two language models, less consistently in two supervised vision transformers, whose failures come late in depth, and rarely in FT-Transformer on tabular data; in DINOv2 and the language models the special tokens — cls, registers, separators — account for almost all failures. (iii) The observation that testing attention averaged over inputs instead, a natural alternative, can both create and destroy exactness. (iv) Two supporting measurements: the classical entry-wise bound κ⁡(A)≤1−N​ε\kappa(A)\leq 1-N\varepsilon is far looser than κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) itself for the numbers of tokens used in real transformers, and the Dobrushin coefficient of DINOv2’s attention averaged over heads and images is often attained at a pair involving a single register token, and drops markedly when that token is left out.

Section 2 fixes notation and modelling choices, Section 3 proves the characterisation, Section 4 reports the measurements, Section 5 discusses limitations and future work, and Section 6 positions the work.

2 Setup

We adopt the setting and notation of Biccari et al. (2026) throughout.

A transformer layer acts on a matrix X∈ℝN×DX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} whose NN rows are token representations of width DD. Each layer adds its output to XX rather than replacing it, X↦X+Layer⁡(X)X\mapsto X+\mathrm{Layer}(X) — a residual, or skip, connection — so the representation passed from layer to layer, called the residual stream, accumulates the contributions of every layer. Self-attention with HH heads computes, for head hh, queries, keys and values Qh=X​WhQQ_{h}=XW_{h}^{Q}, Kh=X​WhKK_{h}=XW_{h}^{K}, Vh=X​WhVV_{h}=XW_{h}^{V} with WhQ,WhK,WhV∈ℝD×dhW_{h}^{Q},W_{h}^{K},W_{h}^{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d_{h}}, where dhd_{h} is the per-head query/key dimension (dh=D/Hd_{h}=D/H when the heads partition the width evenly, as in the models studied here), and the attention matrix

Ah=softmax⁡(Qh​Kh⊤/dh)∈ℝN×N,A_{h}=\operatorname{softmax}\!\big(Q_{h}K_{h}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{h}}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, (1)

row-wise, so that Ah​𝟏=𝟏A_{h}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1} and (Ah)i​k≥0(A_{h})_{ik}\geq 0: each row is a probability distribution over tokens. The head’s contribution to the residual stream is Ah​Vh​WhOA_{h}V_{h}W_{h}^{O}, where WhOW_{h}^{O} is head hh’s slice of the output projection, WhO∈ℝdh×DW_{h}^{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times D}; the layer sums these over heads, adds the result to XX through the residual connection, and follows with normalisation and an MLP. Throughout, NN denotes the number of tokens.

Let A(ℓ)A^{(\ell)} denote the (head-averaged, see (M2)) attention matrix of layer ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L, and A~(ℓ)=(1−α)​I+α​A(ℓ)\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha A^{(\ell)} the corresponding residual factor. The depth-ordered product

RL=A~(L)A~(L−1)⋯A~(1)R_{L}\;=\;\widetilde{A}^{(L)}\widetilde{A}^{(L-1)}\cdots\widetilde{A}^{(1)} (2)

is the transition matrix of a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain on the token index (the layer applied first stands rightmost, since in this model representations propagate as X(ℓ)=A~(ℓ)​X(ℓ−1)X^{(\ell)}=\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}X^{(\ell-1)}); at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} it is attention rollout (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020), and at α=1\alpha=1 the pure-attention product. Rank collapse — all tokens converging to a common representation — is then the weak ergodicity of that chain: the rows of RLR_{L} becoming identical.

Dobrushin’s ergodicity coefficient (Dobrushin, 1956; Seneta, 2006) of a row-stochastic AA is

κ(A)=12maxi,j∥Ai⋅−Aj⋅∥1= 1−mini,j∑kmin(Ai​k,Aj​k)∈[0,1],\kappa(A)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\max_{i,j}\big\|A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}\big\|_{1}\;=\;1-\min_{i,j}\sum_{k}\min\!\big(A_{ik},A_{jk}\big)\;\in\;[0,1], (3)

with κ⁡(A)=0\kappa(A)=0 iff all rows coincide (i.e. AA has rank one).22 2 We write κ\kappa following Biccari et al. (2026); the Markov-chain literature (Seneta, 2006; Ipsen and Selee, 2011) writes τ1\tau_{1} for the same quantity. Two properties make it useful here: it contracts oscillation osc⁡(x)=maxk⁡xk−mink⁡xk\operatorname{osc}(x)=\max_{k}x_{k}-\min_{k}x_{k}, in the sense that osc⁡(A​x)≤κ⁡(A)​osc⁡(x)\operatorname{osc}(Ax)\leq\kappa(A)\operatorname{osc}(x), and it is submultiplicative: for any row-stochastic M(1),…,M(L)M^{(1)},\dots,M^{(L)},

κ(M(L)⋯M(1))≤∏ℓ=1Lκ(M(ℓ)).\kappa\big(M^{(L)}\cdots M^{(1)}\big)\;\leq\;\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\kappa\big(M^{(\ell)}\big). (4)

We state it for general factors because it is applied below both to the attention matrices A(ℓ)A^{(\ell)} and to the residual factors A~(ℓ)\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}. Both are classical (Seneta, 2006). We also use that κ\kappa is convex in AA, which is immediate from (3): κ\kappa is a maximum of the convex functions A↦12∥Ai⋅−Aj⋅∥1A\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\|A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}\|_{1}.

Terminology.

We use a few terms in their technical senses. For a row vector, ‖x‖1=∑k|xk|\|x\|_{1}=\sum_{k}|x_{k}|; since attention rows are probability distributions, 12∥Ai⋅−Aj⋅∥1\tfrac{1}{2}\|A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}\|_{1} is the total-variation distance33 3 In the usual convention, TV⁡(p,q)=maxS⁡|p⁡(S)−q⁡(S)|=12​‖p−q‖1\mathrm{TV}(p,q)=\max_{S}|p(S)-q(S)|=\tfrac{1}{2}\|p-q\|_{1}; some authors call ‖p−q‖1\|p-q\|_{1} itself the total variation. between the distributions of tokens ii and jj, so κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) is the total-variation distance between the two most dissimilar attention rows. A pair (i,j)(i,j) attains κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) when it realises that maximum; the coefficient is decided entirely by such argmax pairs, and all other tokens are invisible to it. Concretely, the contraction property osc⁡(A​x)≤κ⁡(A)​osc⁡(x)\operatorname{osc}(Ax)\leq\kappa(A)\operatorname{osc}(x) says that, for any vector xx with one value per token, the gap between the largest and smallest value across tokens after mixing by AA is at most κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) times what it was. At the level of token mixing, the residual connection makes the operator acting on the residual stream the convex combination A~=(1−α)​I+α​A\widetilde{A}=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha A rather than AA itself, which is why every statement below is about A~\widetilde{A}. By a certificate we mean a bound computable from forward passes alone, without training or search. An attention sink (Xiao et al., 2024) is a token receiving disproportionate attention from many others. Finally, κ\kappa relates to the more familiar spectral notion by κ⁡(A)≥|λ2​(A)|\kappa(A)\geq|\lambda_{2}(A)| (Seneta, 1979), where λ2​(A)\lambda_{2}(A) is the eigenvalue of second-largest modulus (the largest is 11), so 1−κ⁡(A)1-\kappa(A) lower-bounds the spectral gap. The advantage of κ\kappa over the spectral gap here is that it is submultiplicative over different matrices, which is what a product of distinct layers requires.

Equation (4) is a per-layer certificate obtained from a single forward pass. Crucially it requires no time-homogeneity: it holds for arbitrary distinct A(ℓ)A^{(\ell)}, unlike results that assume the same parameters at every layer in order to reach an asymptotic limit (Geshkovski et al., 2023; Vo et al., 2025).

Modelling choices.

These are choices, not theorems, and every claim below is scoped to them.

  1. (M1)

    A transformer layer is not a stochastic matrix. Only the token-mixing part is; the output projection WOW^{O}, the MLP and the normalisation lie outside the certificate.

  2. (M2)

    With HH heads the layer is not a single chain: each head has its own row-stochastic matrix AhA_{h}. Following Biccari et al. (2026), every statement about a layer in Sections 3 and 4 refers to the head average A¯=1H​∑hAh\bar{A}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h}A_{h}, which is again row-stochastic, and by convexity κ⁡(A¯)≤1H​∑hκ⁡(Ah)\kappa(\bar{A})\leq\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h}\kappa(A_{h}). Exactness, however, is not preserved by averaging: it can hold for A¯\bar{A} while failing for individual heads. We therefore also test the individual heads (Section 4.1).

  3. (M3)

    The residual branch is modelled as A~=(1−α)​I+α​A\widetilde{A}=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha A. At α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} this is exactly a rollout factor (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020; Biccari et al., 2026); we keep general α\alpha because Proposition 2 holds for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), not only for α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}. DINOv2 uses LayerScale (a learned per-channel multiplier on each branch), so the effective residual weight is not literally 12\tfrac{1}{2}.

  4. (M4)

    We test the content subchain: the submatrix of A¯\bar{A} on the content tokens alone — image patches, words, or tabular features — discarding the special tokens, namely the cls token of the image models and of FT-Transformer, the four registers of the DINOv2 models that have them, and the classification and separator tokens [CLS] and [SEP] of the language models (<s> and </s> in RoBERTa), with the remaining rows rescaled to sum to one. For images we also call it the patch subchain. This is a choice about which tokens enter each attention matrix, separate from how many inputs the matrix is averaged over. The subchain is a different Markov chain from the original, not a restriction of it — deleting states and renormalising changes the dynamics — so results on it do not transfer automatically to the full token set. We report every model on both, and the difference is itself informative (Section 4). Because rescaling the rows does not commute with averaging, we apply the restriction only after all averaging: over heads and, where applicable (Section 4.2), over inputs as well.

3 The residual bound and when it is attained

Lemma 1 (Residual bound; Biccari et al., 2026, eq. (A.6) at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}).

For row-stochastic AA and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], with A~=(1−α)​I+α​A\widetilde{A}=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha A,

κ⁡(A~)≤(1−α)+α​κ​(A).\kappa(\widetilde{A})\;\leq\;(1-\alpha)+\alpha\,\kappa(A). (5)
Proof.

κ\kappa is convex on the set of row-stochastic matrices and κ⁡(I)=1\kappa(I)=1, so κ⁡((1−α)​I+α​A)≤(1−α)​κ​(I)+α​κ​(A)\kappa((1-\alpha)I+\alpha A)\leq(1-\alpha)\kappa(I)+\alpha\kappa(A). At α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} this recovers the estimate of Biccari et al. (2026), obtained there by the triangle inequality. ∎

At α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}, Biccari et al. (2026) compose their case of Lemma 1 across depth into

κ⁡(RL)≤∏ℓ=1Lκ⁡(A~(ℓ))≤ 2−L​∏ℓ=1L(1+κ⁡(A(ℓ))),\kappa(R_{L})\;\leq\;\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\kappa\big(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}\big)\;\leq\;2^{-L}\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\big(1+\kappa(A^{(\ell)})\big), (6)

and separately prove the unconditional floor κ⁡(A~)≥(N−2)/(2​(N−1))\kappa(\widetilde{A})\geq(N-2)/(2(N-1)),44 4 In their notation, dd stands for NN. which tends to 12\tfrac{1}{2} as the number of tokens grows. We state the results below for every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), which the proof allows at no extra cost; all our measurements use α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}.

The interesting question is when the second inequality — the layerwise estimate — is tight, since that determines whether the certificate is informative or merely valid.

Proposition 2 (Exactness).

Let AA be row-stochastic and 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Then

κ⁡(A~)=(1−α)+α​κ​(A)\kappa(\widetilde{A})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\,\kappa(A) (7)

if and only if there exists a pair (i,j)(i,j) attaining 12∥Ai⋅−Aj⋅∥1=κ(A)\tfrac{1}{2}\|A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}\|_{1}=\kappa(A) that satisfies

Ai​i≥Aj​iandAj​j≥Ai​j.A_{ii}\ \geq\ A_{ji}\qquad\text{and}\qquad A_{jj}\ \geq\ A_{ij}. (8)
Proof.

Fix i≠ji\neq j and write d=Ai⋅−Aj⋅d=A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}, so di=Ai​i−Aj​id_{i}=A_{ii}-A_{ji} and dj=Ai​j−Aj​jd_{j}=A_{ij}-A_{jj}. Then

A~i⋅−A~j⋅=(1−α)(ei−ej)+αd,\widetilde{A}_{i\cdot}-\widetilde{A}_{j\cdot}=(1-\alpha)(e_{i}-e_{j})+\alpha d,

with eie_{i} the ii-th canonical basis vector, whose coordinates are (1−α)+α​di(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_{i} at position ii, −(1−α)+α​dj-(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_{j} at position jj, and α​dk\alpha d_{k} elsewhere. By the triangle inequality,

12∥A~i⋅−A~j⋅∥1\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl\|\widetilde{A}_{i\cdot}-\widetilde{A}_{j\cdot}\bigr\|_{1} =12​(|(1−α)+α​di|+|(1−α)−α​dj|+α​∑k≠i,j|dk|)\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(\bigl|(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_{i}\bigr|+\bigl|(1-\alpha)-\alpha d_{j}\bigr|+\alpha\textstyle\sum_{k\neq i,j}|d_{k}|\Bigr)
≤(1−α)+α⋅12​‖d‖1≤(1−α)+α​κ​(A).\displaystyle\leq(1-\alpha)+\alpha\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\|d\|_{1}\;\leq\;(1-\alpha)+\alpha\,\kappa(A).

The first inequality holds term by term: since 1−α>01-\alpha>0, |(1−α)+α​di|≤(1−α)+α​|di|\bigl|(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_{i}\bigr|\leq(1-\alpha)+\alpha|d_{i}| with equality if and only if di≥0d_{i}\geq 0, and |(1−α)−α​dj|≤(1−α)+α​|dj|\bigl|(1-\alpha)-\alpha d_{j}\bigr|\leq(1-\alpha)+\alpha|d_{j}| with equality if and only if dj≤0d_{j}\leq 0 (as |x+y|=|x|+|y||x+y|=|x|+|y| if and only if x​y≥0xy\geq 0). So the first inequality is an equality if and only if (i,j)(i,j) satisfies (8), and the second if and only if (i,j)(i,j) attains κ⁡(A)\kappa(A).

If some κ⁡(A)\kappa(A)-attaining pair satisfies (8), equality holds throughout for it; since the chain bounds every pair, κ⁡(A~)=(1−α)+α​κ​(A)\kappa(\widetilde{A})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A).

Conversely, if κ⁡(A~)=(1−α)+α​κ​(A)\kappa(\widetilde{A})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A), equality holds throughout for any pair attaining κ⁡(A~)\kappa(\widetilde{A}), which has i≠ji\neq j because this value is positive; as α>0\alpha>0, that pair attains κ⁡(A)\kappa(A) and satisfies (8). ∎

Example 3 (The bound can fail completely).

Let A=(0110)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}, the two-token swap. Its rows are disjoint, so κ⁡(A)=1\kappa(A)=1 and Lemma 1 gives only the trivial bound κ⁡(A~)≤1\kappa(\widetilde{A})\leq 1. But A~=12​(I+A)=(1/21/21/21/2)\widetilde{A}=\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A)=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\ 1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix} has identical rows, hence κ⁡(A~)=0\kappa(\widetilde{A})=0: the residual destroys the entire difference instead of preserving half of it. The condition fails at the only attaining pair, since A11=0<1=A21A_{11}=0<1=A_{21}.

Remark 1 (Interpretation).

Condition (8) says that each of the two extremal tokens attends to itself at least as strongly as the other extremal token attends to it — a mutual self-dominance of a pair that realises the coefficient (the pair need not be unique; the condition asks this of some attaining pair, not of all). The residual scales every row by α\alpha and adds mass 1−α1-\alpha to its diagonal entry; mutual self-dominance is precisely the condition under which, for that pair, the added mass reinforces the existing difference between the two rows rather than partially cancelling it. Example 3 is the opposite extreme, where it cancels the difference entirely. The condition fails at a pair when one of its two tokens receives more attention from the other than it pays itself — a pattern that an attention sink, receiving attention from many tokens, can produce when it is one of the pair.

Remark 2 (Size of a failure).

The computation in the proof also bounds the size of a failure. For any pair (i,j)(i,j) attaining κ⁡(A)\kappa(A),

0≤(1−α)+α​κ​(A)−κ⁡(A~)≤α⁡[(Aj​i−Ai​i)++(Ai​j−Aj​j)+],0\leq(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A)-\kappa(\widetilde{A})\leq\alpha\bigl[(A_{ji}-A_{ii})^{+}+(A_{ij}-A_{jj})^{+}\bigr],

and the bound on the gap is sharp: in Example 3 both sides equal 11. A failure is therefore never larger than α\alpha times the total amount by which the two inequalities of (8) fail, and each of these amounts is at most one attention entry. When attention is spread over many tokens its entries are small, and so are its failures: uniformly random matrices with 256256 tokens (the uniform model below) fail condition (8) about three times in four, but at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} by a median gap of only 0.5%0.5\% of 12​κ​(A)\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa(A).

Corollary 1 (Factorwise tightness).

Let 0<α<10<\alpha<1. If the condition of Proposition 2 holds at every layer, then κ⁡(A~(ℓ))=(1−α)+α​κ​(A(ℓ))\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A^{(\ell)}) for all ℓ\ell. In particular, at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} the second inequality in (6) is an equality:

∏ℓ=1Lκ⁡(A~(ℓ))= 2−L​∏ℓ=1L(1+κ⁡(A(ℓ))).\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\kappa\big(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}\big)\;=\;2^{-L}\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\big(1+\kappa(A^{(\ell)})\big).

The depth certificate (6) bounds κ⁡(RL)\kappa(R_{L}) in two steps: submultiplicativity, κ⁡(RL)≤∏ℓκ⁡(A~(ℓ))\kappa(R_{L})\leq\prod_{\ell}\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}), and then the layerwise estimate applied to each factor. Under the condition the second step is an equality at every layer, so the certificate cannot be improved by sharpening the layerwise estimate. Whatever gap remains between the certificate and κ⁡(RL)\kappa(R_{L}) comes from the first step, which is typically strict: the coefficient of a product of matrices is usually much smaller than the product of their coefficients. A tighter certificate would have to use more information about the attention matrices than their coefficients.

Condition (8) cannot be dropped: without it the bound can fail, and Example 3 shows that it can fail by the largest possible amount. How often random matrices satisfy the condition depends on how they are generated, so we use three random models, each at N=4N=4, 88, 3232, 128128 and 256256 tokens with 10001000 matrices per size. Under the uniform model each row is a random probability vector, with all probability vectors equally likely: it is drawn independently from the uniform distribution on the probability simplex {p∈ℝN:pk≥0,∑kpk=1}\{p\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:p_{k}\geq 0,\ \sum_{k}p_{k}=1\} (the Dirichlet distribution with all parameters equal to one); under the softmax model each row is the softmax of independent standard Gaussian logits. Both satisfy the condition in only 2424–30%30\% of cases, at every size. The third model imitates two features common in trained attention: every token sends an extra share of its attention to one common sink token, and an extra share to itself. Row ii is (1−a−b)​ui+a​es+b​ei(1-a-b)\,u_{i}+a\,e_{s}+b\,e_{i}, where uiu_{i} is a random row drawn from the uniform model, ese_{s} and eie_{i} are the unit vectors of the sink token ss, chosen uniformly at random, and of token ii, and a,b∈[0,12]a,b\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}] are the weights of the two extra shares. Since a+b≤1a+b\leq 1, each row is again a probability vector. The weights are drawn once per matrix, since a sink attracts attention from every token of a head; to include matrices with neither feature, either one, or both, aa and bb are drawn independently, each equal to zero with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2} and otherwise uniform on [0,12][0,\tfrac{1}{2}]. The extra weight on the diagonal favours the condition, which asks each extremal token to attend to itself at least as strongly as the other attends to it, and the condition now holds in 5858–63%63\% of cases. The exact rate depends on these choices; the point is that building in self-preference makes the condition more common, but still far from certain. It is therefore not automatic, which is what makes its behaviour in trained models (Section 4) a substantive observation rather than a restatement of Lemma 1.

Two remarks delimit what the depth bound can say. It is one-sided: a small product of layer coefficients shows that the rollout is close to rank one, but a large product shows nothing, since κ⁡(RL)\kappa(R_{L}) can lie far below it. And where the condition fails the per-layer estimate is loose, so the bound understates how much such a layer mixes: a failure of the condition is a limitation of the bound, not a property of the network.

4 Empirical results

What is tested.

In the bound of Biccari et al. (2026), the layerwise estimate is applied to one input at a time. For each input xx, the heads of layer ℓ\ell are averaged into the input-dependent matrix A¯(ℓ)​(x)\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x), and the coefficient of that input’s rollout is bounded by (6). For a dataset, the input-specific rollouts are averaged, and the coefficient of the average is bounded by the average of the right-hand sides of (6), as in their (A.7) and (A.8). Each factor 12​(1+κ⁡(A¯(ℓ)​(x)))\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1+\kappa(\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x))\big) in these bounds is the layerwise estimate of Lemma 1 applied to the matrix of one input at one layer. Whether their estimate is tight is therefore a question about the matrices A¯(ℓ)​(x)\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x) of individual inputs, and this is our primary test: for every input and layer we evaluate the gap of Proposition 2 on that input’s head-averaged matrix, and report the share of input–layer pairs at which the bound is attained, that is, at which condition (8) holds. Averaging over the inputs before testing gives a different object, ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle, the mean of A¯(ℓ)​(x)\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x) over the inputs, which behaves differently; we report it separately (Section 4.2).

Models and data.

We test DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) in its released variant with register tokens, at three sizes (ViT-S/14, ViT-B/14 and ViT-L/14, with 1212, 1212 and 2424 layers), and, as a control, the ViT-B/14 variant trained without them. Register tokens are extra learnable vectors appended to the input sequence that correspond to no image patch: Darcet et al. (2024) introduced them because vision transformers otherwise repurpose a few patch tokens to carry high-norm global information. We further test two ViT-B/16 models trained with supervision on ImageNet, the original ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and DeiT-B (Touvron et al., 2021), and the bidirectional language encoders RoBERTa-base (Liu et al., 2019) and DistilBERT (Sanh et al., 2019). Image models are evaluated on 512512 images drawn at random from ImageNetV2 (Recht et al., 2019), language models on 512512 sequences of exactly 128128 tokens with no padding, drawn at random from the training split of WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017), so that every attention row is a distribution over the full sequence. For every model we test attention among the content tokens, image patches, words or tabular features. The special tokens — the cls token, the registers, and the classification and separator tokens [CLS] and [SEP] (<s> and </s> in RoBERTa) — remain part of the model and influence its attention, but they are removed from the matrices we test, which is the content subchain of (M4). We also test every model on all of its tokens; the difference shows where the condition breaks. We chose bidirectional encoders rather than decoder-only models such as GPT-2 for a reason specific to the coefficient. In a decoder-only model each token may attend only to itself and earlier tokens, so the first token attends only to itself: its attention row is e1=(1,0,…,0)e_{1}=(1,0,\dots,0). That row overlaps any other row jj only in Aj​1A_{j1}, the attention token jj pays to the first position, so by the second form of (3), κ⁡(A)≥1−minj⁡Aj​1\kappa(A)\geq 1-\min_{j}A_{j1}. The next rows are constrained in the same way, more weakly: row ii can overlap another row only on the first ii positions. The coefficient is therefore governed by how much the tokens attend to the first few positions, a consequence of the mask, rather than by mixing across the sequence.

Sample size and precision.

The shares in Table 1 use 512512 inputs per pretrained model. Larger samples give the same picture: on all 10 00010\,000 images of ImageNetV2 for DINOv2-B, DeiT-B and ViT-B/16, and on 40964096 sequences for RoBERTa, the overall share changes by at most 0.20.2 percentage points and the share at any single layer by at most 2.62.6; in particular, DINOv2-B fails at no layer beyond the first for any of the 10 00010\,000 images.55 5 The larger samples also reveal failures too rare for 512512 inputs to detect at two further layers: in 44 of 10 00010\,000 images at layer 66 of ViT-B/16, and in 22 at layer 1010 of DeiT-B. We count a gap as zero when it is below 10−1010^{-10}; Appendix B explains this choice and shows that the counts barely depend on it.

4.1 The condition on each input’s attention

In DINOv2 the condition holds for essentially every image at every layer (Table 1): at 24 56624\,566 of the 24 57624\,576 image–layer pairs of DINOv2-S, -B and -L, the variants trained with registers, against the 2424–30%30\% at which random matrices satisfy it (Section 3). All ten failures are at layer 11 — unlike those of the other encoders below, which come late in depth — and all are small. We measure the size of a failure by its gap as a fraction of 12​κ​(A¯)\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa(\bar{A}), the part of the bound that depends on the attention: under exactness, at our α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}, κ⁡(A~)=12+12​κ​(A¯)\kappa(\widetilde{A})=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa(\bar{A}), and the constant 12\tfrac{1}{2} comes from the skip connection and is the same for every matrix. By this measure, at each of the ten failures the bound overstates the attention’s part by at most 3%3\%, and their gaps, between 3.6×10−53.6\times 10^{-5} and 3.6×10−33.6\times 10^{-3}, are far above numerical precision (Appendix B). DINOv2-B trained without registers behaves the same way, so training with registers is not what makes the patch subchain exact. The two language models behave like DINOv2 on their content tokens: RoBERTa satisfies the condition at 6 1256\,125 of its 6 1446\,144 sequence–layer pairs and DistilBERT at all 3 0723\,072.

The two supervised vision transformers are the exception. Even on their patch tokens the condition fails for some inputs, late in depth (Figure 1): in DeiT-B at layer 1111 for 10%10\% of images and at layer 1212 for all of them, and in ViT-B/16 for most images at layers 88, 99, 1010 and 1212, and for 27%27\% and 46%46\% of them at layers 77 and 1111. Most of these failures are small in the sense just defined: at the median failure the bound overstates the attention’s part by 1.6%1.6\% in DeiT-B and 3.7%3.7\% in ViT-B/16. With so many tokens this is expected rather than informative (Remark 2): what distinguishes trained attention is how often the gap is exactly zero. We do not know why they arise late in depth, or why only in these two models.

Special tokens are where the condition breaks.

Including the special tokens changes the picture for DINOv2 and the language models (Table 1, bottom row of Figure 1). On all tokens, DINOv2 with registers satisfies the condition for only 8282–91%91\% of image–layer pairs: at layer 11 nearly every image fails, and in the later layers of DINOv2-B and -L many do. RoBERTa and DistilBERT drop to 90%90\% and 97%97\%, failing mainly at layers 99 and 1212 and at layer 66 respectively; removing the two special tokens of each sequence, which leaves only its 126126 text tokens, removes 713713 of the 732732 failures. This is consistent with the observation of Clark et al. (2019) that over half of BERT’s attention in layers 66 to 1010 goes to [SEP]. Without registers, the cls token alone lowers DINOv2-B to 97%97\%, mostly at layer 1111. In the two supervised vision transformers, by contrast, including the cls token changes almost nothing (90.7%90.7\% and 64.1%64.1\% on all tokens, against 90.9%90.9\% and 64.4%64.4\% on patches): their failures lie among the patches themselves.

Individual heads, reported in the last-but-one column of Table 1, satisfy the condition for 6161–97%97\% of head–input–layer triples (one head, at one layer, on one input), far more often than random matrices, so the head average of (M2) is not what produces the result.

What the certificate attains.

For a single image xx, the depth bound (6) of Biccari et al. (2026) is

B⁡(x)=∏ℓ=1L12​(1+κ⁡(A¯(ℓ)​(x))),B(x)\;=\;\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1+\kappa\big(\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x)\big)\Big),

an upper bound on κ​(RL​(x))\kappa(R_{L}(x)), the coefficient of that image’s rollout. For a dataset they bound the coefficient of the averaged rollout ⟨RL⟩\langle R_{L}\rangle, the mean of RL​(x)R_{L}(x) over the images, by the mean of B⁡(x)B(x).

Where condition (8) holds, the corresponding factor of B⁡(x)B(x) is exact; in DINOv2 this is so for all but ten of the 24 57624\,576 factors. Yet the bound remains loose. Over our 512512 images the mean of B⁡(x)B(x) is 0.440.44, 0.360.36 and 0.0650.065 for DINOv2-S, -B and -L, while the coefficient it bounds, κ⁡(⟨RL⟩)\kappa(\langle R_{L}\rangle), is 0.0930.093, 0.0750.075 and 0.00220.0022 on the same images: the bound is five to thirty times too large, although almost every factor in it is exact.

The excess comes from the two other steps in its derivation: submultiplicativity, κ⁡(RL​(x))≤∏ℓκ⁡(A~(ℓ)​(x))\kappa(R_{L}(x))\leq\prod_{\ell}\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)}(x)), since the coefficient of a product of matrices is usually much smaller than the product of their coefficients; and averaging over images, which by convexity can only lower the coefficient.

The attention analysis predicts a collapse that does not happen.

If tokens were mixed by attention alone, as the rollout models them, DINOv2-L would leave every token with nearly the same representation: its rollout over 2424 layers, averaged over images, has coefficient 0.00220.0022, so by Theorem 2.3 of Biccari et al. (2026) it is close to a matrix whose rows are all equal — one that gives every token the same weighted average of the inputs. Yet DINOv2-L does not collapse. Its patch features support per-pixel tasks such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation from a single image (Oquab et al., 2024), which would be impossible if the patch tokens had become interchangeable. The resolution lies in what the rollout leaves out. It tracks only the attention matrices, so the value projections, the MLP and the normalisation lie outside it (M1), and it weights the residual branch by 12\tfrac{1}{2}, whereas DINOv2 weights it by learned per-channel factors (M3). Whatever keeps the representations apart must lie in these parts of the network. This is a caution about the rollout framework itself — ours and Biccari et al. (2026)’s alike — rather than a finding about DINOv2: a near-collapsed rollout is compatible with a model that is working perfectly well.

4.2 Averaging over inputs

Averaging attention over inputs before testing is natural when one wants to describe a layer’s typical attention pattern. The last column of Table 1 reports it: for each model ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle is formed from the same inputs and tested. On content tokens, the averaged matrices of the eight pretrained models satisfy the condition at 100100 of their 102102 layers; the two exceptions are the last layers of DeiT-B and ViT-B/16. This verdict is stable: on the larger samples of Section 4 — all 10 00010\,000 images for DINOv2-B, DeiT-B and ViT-B/16, and 40964096 sequences for RoBERTa — it is the same at every layer, and for all three DINOv2 models also over five independent draws of 512512 images.

But the averaged test answers a different question, and it can agree or disagree with the per-input test, because exactness is not preserved by averaging in either direction. In ViT-B/16 the averaged matrix is exact at layers 77 to 1111, although 27%27\% to 88%88\% of individual images fail there: averaging creates exactness. In RoBERTa on all tokens, 509509 of 512512 sequences are exact at layer 88, but the averaged matrix is not (its gap is 7.4×10−37.4\times 10^{-3}): averaging destroys it. Averaging also lowers the coefficient. For DINOv2-B, ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle has κ\kappa between 0.190.19 and 0.780.78 across layers, while the median over images of the per-image coefficient κ​(A¯(ℓ)​(x))\kappa(\bar{A}^{(\ell)}(x)) lies between 0.430.43 and 0.940.94, because an average of attention patterns is more uniform than the patterns themselves. The coefficient of an averaged matrix describes how much the typical pattern mixes, not how much the attention of any input does.

Individual heads averaged over inputs, on content tokens, are exact for 570570 of the 600600 DINOv2 heads, 141141 of 144144 in RoBERTa and 7070 of 7272 in DistilBERT. On all tokens the averaged matrices fail more often, as the per-input test does: at five of the twelve layers of DINOv2-B, for instance, each time with a register in the extremal pair.

Column dominance is sufficient but not the explanation.

One simple sufficient condition exists. If every diagonal entry is the largest in its column — Ai​i≥Ak​iA_{ii}\geq A_{ki} for all ii and kk, so that no token attends to ii more strongly than ii attends to itself — then both inequalities of (8) hold at every pair, and exactness follows whichever pair attains κ\kappa. The property is demanding: among the uniform and softmax random matrices of Section 3, none of the 10001000 at each of 88, 3232, 128128 and 256256 tokens has it. It is common among the DINOv2 heads averaged over images, ⟨Ah(ℓ)⟩\langle A_{h}^{(\ell)}\rangle: 308308 of the 600600 have it, and all of them satisfy condition (8), as the argument requires. But it does not explain the regularity: 262262 of the 570570 heads that satisfy the condition lack it, and ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle satisfies the condition at all 4848 layers of the three models, although it is column dominant at only 2929 of them, and at four of them not in a single column. Which property governs the condition remains open.

4.3 A contrasting case: FT-Transformer

Condition (8) is not universal. We trained FT-Transformer (Gorishniy et al., 2021), a widely used transformer architecture for tabular data, on two standard benchmarks, California Housing (Pace and Barry, 1997) with 88 features and Higgs (Baldi et al., 2014) with 2828, using its authors’ own data splits, preprocessing and default configuration of three blocks, and additionally with six blocks on California Housing; its tokens are one cls token and one token per feature, 99 in all on California Housing and 2929 on Higgs (details in Appendix A). The models reproduce the authors’ own results: on Higgs our three seeds reach 0.7250.725–0.7280.728 accuracy against their 0.7210.721–0.7240.724, and on California Housing they come within about 0.010.01 of their RMSE. Yet per input, on its feature tokens, condition (8) holds for only 1111–44%44\% of input–layer pairs, and for 1010–32%32\% with the cls token included (Table 1): far below the other models, and in two of the three configurations, both on California Housing, below the rate for random matrices. Few tokens do not by themselves explain this: random matrices satisfy the condition about as often with few tokens as with many (Section 3). The size of the failures depends on the dataset: at the median failure the bound overstates the attention’s part of the coefficient, 12​κ​(A¯)\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa(\bar{A}), by 5%5\% on Higgs and by 2323–38%38\% on California Housing. These larger failures are consistent with Remark 2: with only 2929 or 99 tokens, single attention entries are large.

4.4 The entry-wise route does not bind at realistic numbers of tokens

Some asymptotic arguments that attention mixes tokens rest on a lower bound, uniform over all layers, for the entries of the attention matrices. Wu et al. (2023), for instance, use a constant ε>0\varepsilon>0 bounding every entry of every attention matrix from below, which they show exists (their Lemma 2). Such an ε\varepsilon bounds the coefficient directly: if every entry is at least ε\varepsilon, any two rows overlap in at least N​εN\varepsilon, so by the second form of (3), κ⁡(A)=1−min⁡∑ki,j⁡min⁡(Ai​k,Aj​k)≤1−N​ε\kappa(A)=1-\min_{i,j}\sum_{k}\min(A_{ik},A_{jk})\leq 1-N\varepsilon — the classical Doeblin bound. The question is how large ε\varepsilon is in a real transformer.

It is small. We measure it on the patch subchain of DINOv2, in the case most favourable to the entry-wise route: the matrix ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle, whose smallest entry is at least the smallest entry over all individual heads and inputs, because averaging fills in near-zero entries. Even there the Doeblin bound is loose rather than informative: it exceeds the directly computed coefficient of that matrix, κ⁡(⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩)\kappa(\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle), at every layer (Figure 2), by a factor between 1.061.06 and 4.54.5, and on average by 2424 to 41%41\% per layer in the three models, an excess that compounds over depth. The bound that the asymptotic arguments need must hold for every head and every input at once; its ε\varepsilon can therefore be no larger than the smallest entry in this favourable case, and the bound it gives can only be looser. This is not a defect in the asymptotic results, which concern limits and are correct as such; it is a statement about what the same quantity can certify for the number of tokens of a deployed model.

4.5 When one token carries the coefficient

Because κ⁡(A)=maxi⁡ci\kappa(A)=\max_{i}c_{i} with ci:=maxj12∥Ai⋅−Aj⋅∥1c_{i}:=\max_{j}\tfrac{1}{2}\|A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}\|_{1}, the coefficient decomposes over tokens. A sharper question is which tokens are load-bearing: with κ−i(A):=12maxj,k≠i∥Aj⋅−Ak⋅∥1\kappa_{-i}(A):=\tfrac{1}{2}\max_{j,k\neq i}\|A_{j\cdot}-A_{k\cdot}\|_{1} — the coefficient restricted to pairs avoiding token ii, rows unchanged, not the deleted-and-renormalised submatrix — define Δi:=κ⁡(A)−κ−i​(A)\Delta_{i}:=\kappa(A)-\kappa_{-i}(A), the drop when token ii is barred from the maximum. By construction Δi>0\Delta_{i}>0 only for tokens belonging to every κ\kappa-attaining pair, so at most two tokens have a positive score.

We apply it to ⟨A¯(ℓ)⟩\langle\bar{A}^{(\ell)}\rangle on the full DINOv2 token set, registers included, and call the token with the largest Δi\Delta_{i} the layer’s carrier. The top carriers fall into two well-separated groups (Table 2, Figure 3). At roughly half the layers of each model the carrier is a register or cls token with Δ\Delta up to 0.160.16; at the others it is an ordinary patch with Δ\Delta of at most a few thousandths, meaning that no single token matters. In the sample of Table 2 and Figure 3 the two groups overlap only at layer 2323 of DINOv2-L, where a register carries Δ=1.8×10−3\Delta=1.8\times 10^{-3}; in four further independent draws of 512512 images, cls carries that layer and the groups do not overlap. The carrier is also usually one specific register (Table 2, last column), and this is stable across the five draws: the modal register is the same in every draw for all three models, and the carrier token itself is identical across draws at all 1212 layers of DINOv2-S and at 2323 of the 2424 layers of DINOv2-L. The other registers and cls carry the rest. The four register tokens (Darcet et al., 2024) are therefore not interchangeable with respect to mixing.

5 Limitations and future work

The exactness result is an empirical regularity, not a property of trained transformers in general. On content tokens it holds for essentially every input in DINOv2 and the two language models we test; the two supervised vision transformers fail it for some inputs late in depth, including the special tokens breaks it in DINOv2 and the language models, and FT-Transformer trained on tabular data largely lacks it. We do not know what governs it — why the special tokens break it, or why the supervised models fail late — and column dominance, the obvious candidate, is sufficient but does not explain it (Section 4.2). The evidence has further limits. Each pretrained model is tested on one dataset, and the tabular evidence rests on one architecture and two datasets. The residual weight α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} follows Biccari et al. (2026) (M3), and the main results concern content tokens (M4). We have not tested decoder-only models, where causal masking changes what the coefficient measures (Section 4).

Three directions follow. The first is to explain the pattern: to find the property of trained attention that the condition tracks, why the special tokens break it, and why it fails late in depth in the supervised vision transformers but not in DINOv2. A related question is whether the columns in which column dominance fails can locate such tokens — attention sinks, or the high-norm artefact patches of models trained without registers (Darcet et al., 2024) — from attention alone. The second is to widen the evidence, to further tabular architectures such as TabPFN and to larger and decoder-only language models. The third is practical: the coefficient can be computed from the attention matrices of a single forward pass, and we plan to examine whether it can support more efficient training or the pruning of attention heads.

6 Related work

Direct antecedent.

Biccari et al. (2026) apply Doeblin–Dobrushin contraction theory to attention rollout in tabular transformers, and the framing adopted here is theirs: the Dobrushin coefficient of the head-averaged attention matrix, the residual modelled as 12​(I+A)\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A), the layerwise estimate κ⁡(12​(I+A))≤12​(1+κ⁡(A))\kappa(\tfrac{1}{2}(I+A))\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\kappa(A)) (their (A.6), our Lemma 1) and its composition over depth, the entry-wise bound κ≤1−N​ε\kappa\leq 1-N\varepsilon (their Proposition A.2), and the observation that the coefficient decreases with depth. Their principal result, Theorem 2.3, shows that a rollout with a small coefficient is close to a rank-one matrix. We take up a question their treatment leaves open: they bound the coefficient of each residual factor from above, κ⁡(A~(ℓ))≤12​(1+κ⁡(A(ℓ)))\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)})\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1+\kappa(A^{(\ell)})\big) (their (A.6)), but do not determine when this bound is attained. Proposition 2 answers that question, and Corollary 1 turns the answer into a statement about their depth bound.

Rank collapse and oversmoothing.

That pure self-attention loses rank with depth is established: Dong et al. (2021) show doubly exponential convergence to a rank-one matrix, and identify residual connections and the MLP as what prevents it. The residual connection leaves the same mark on the Dobrushin coefficient of each rollout factor: at α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}, κ⁡(A~(ℓ))≥(N−2)/(2​(N−1))≈12\kappa(\widetilde{A}^{(\ell)})\geq(N-2)/(2(N-1))\approx\tfrac{1}{2} at every layer (Biccari et al., 2026, Lemma A.4), so a bound built layer by layer cannot certify contraction faster than about a factor of two per layer. And Section 4 shows that what prevents collapse lies outside what the rollout models: in DINOv2-L the attention rollout is close to rank one at 2424 layers, yet the representations do not collapse. In the graph setting the same phenomenon is known as oversmoothing (Oono and Suzuki, 2020).

Ergodicity of attention products.

Wu et al. (2023) analyse attention-based graph neural networks as products of inhomogeneous row-stochastic matrices and prove oversmoothing at an exponential rate; transformers fall within their setting as attention on a complete graph. Their analysis concerns the limit of infinite depth; ours concerns the residual factor of each layer at finite depth.

Depth as a dynamical system.

Jacobs et al. (2026) treat ViT depth as a flow and segment it into contiguous phases of reused computation. Vo et al. (2025) characterise token limit points in deep selective SSMs under an assumption of time-independent parameters, and Geshkovski et al. (2023) study clustering in self-attention dynamics in a continuous-time limit. The coefficient used here requires neither homogeneity nor a limit, at the cost of giving a bound rather than a rate.

Ergodicity coefficients.

κ\kappa is due to Dobrushin (1956); weak ergodicity of inhomogeneous chains to Hajnal and Bartlett (1958); Seneta (1979); Seneta (2006) develops the general theory, and Ipsen and Selee (2011) treat the family of coefficients defined by vector norms.

Appendix A FT-Transformer on tabular data

We train FT-Transformer with the authors’ package (Gorishniy et al., 2021) on their own data files, which fix the split of each dataset into training, validation and test sets. Preprocessing follows their code and is the same for both datasets: missing values, where present, are replaced by training-set column means; a small noise of relative size 10−310^{-3} is added to the training features before a quantile transform to a normal distribution is fitted, which breaks ties among repeated values; and the targets of California Housing, the regression task, are standardised. We use their default configuration of three blocks and, on California Housing, also six blocks. In the last block the package computes attention only for the cls token, so that block’s attention is a single row rather than a token-mixing matrix, and we test the other blocks. Training stops once validation performance has not improved for 1616 epochs, with no hyperparameter tuning. Attention is tested on 40004000 test rows, each row being one input: per row, and averaged over rows. We run three seeds per configuration and compare with the authors’ own runs for the same seeds, and with gradient boosting (scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoosting, default settings) and a linear model (linear regression for California Housing, logistic regression for Higgs) fitted on the same split (Table 3).

Appendix B Numerical precision

The models compute attention in single precision, which carries about seven significant digits. Computing the coefficient and the gap in single precision as well would blur exactly the distinction we need: on random matrices of the same size that satisfy the condition, the gap computed in single precision comes out as large as 1.2×10−71.2\times 10^{-7}, the size of the smallest genuine failures we observe, while in double precision it stays below 3×10−163\times 10^{-16}. We therefore convert each attention matrix to double precision, with about sixteen significant digits, before computing its coefficient and gap. The conversion is exact, and a gap that is zero in exact arithmetic then appears as a number of order 10−1610^{-16}, far below any genuine failure.

We count a gap as zero when it is below 10−1010^{-10}. For the head-averaged matrices of the pretrained models this choice hardly matters: of the 562 752562\,752 such gaps we computed, on content tokens and on all tokens, all but one are either below 10−1410^{-14} or at least 10−710^{-7}, so any threshold between those values gives the same counts — a separation that exists only because the gaps are computed in double precision — and the one exception, 6×10−86\times 10^{-8}, alters a single count. For individual heads a few gaps fall in between: moving the threshold anywhere in that range changes the shares by at most 0.250.25 percentage points on content tokens, and by up to 1.61.6 on the full token sets of DINOv2. Finally, as a cross-check, evaluating condition (8) directly, by locating the pairs that attain κ\kappa, gives the same verdict as the gap at all 61446144 image–layer pairs of DINOv2-S and of ViT-B/16 — including the 21902190 pairs of ViT-B/16 at which the condition fails, so the two tests agree where the bound is not attained as well as where it is.

Appendix C Failures layer by layer

Table 4 lists, for each pretrained model of Table 1, the layers at which some input fails condition (8) and the number of failing inputs out of 512512, on content tokens and on all tokens. At every other layer every input satisfies it.

Appendix D Robustness to the input size

Each model was trained at a fixed input size. This appendix therefore does not compare models; it checks, within each model, whether the per-input verdict of Section 4.1 changes when the model is evaluated at other input sizes.

Figure 4 repeats the per-input test on content tokens for DINOv2-B and ViT-B/16 at resolutions of 112112, 224224, 336336 and 448448 pixels (6464–10241024 and 4949–784784 patches), and for the two language models at sequence lengths of 3232, 6464, 128128, 256256 and 512512 tokens (3030–510510 text tokens). We use 256256 images per resolution, which keeps the largest resolutions affordable and at 224224 pixels reproduces the 512512-image shares of Table 1, and 512512 sequences per length. ViT-B/16 was trained at 224224 pixels, and the language models on sequences of up to 512512 tokens.

The verdicts do not change. DINOv2-B is exact at 99.899.8–99.97%99.97\% of image–layer pairs at every resolution, with its few failures confined to layer 11. ViT-B/16 stays between 61%61\% and 65%65\%, failing only at layers 77–1212. DistilBERT remains exact for essentially every input. RoBERTa declines slightly, from 99.97%99.97\% to 98.1%98.1\%, as its failures at layers 99 and 1212 become more frequent with length. The averaged verdict of every model is likewise the same at every input size. Exactness also does not peak at the training size: RoBERTa, trained only on full-length sequences of 512512 tokens (Liu et al., 2019), is exact least often at that length.

What does change is the size of the failures. In ViT-B/16 their median falls from 12.6%12.6\% to 1.2%1.2\% of the attention’s part, 12​κ​(A¯)\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa(\bar{A}), as the number of patches increases, consistent with Remark 2. In RoBERTa the median rises slightly, from 4.2%4.2\% to 5.4%5.4\%: at its failing layers the coefficient is close to 11, so attention there is concentrated, and the bound of Remark 2 does not force the failures to be small.
